It decouples GPU residency from SSD write latency by staging evicted blocks in CPU memory before persisting them, turning frequent small updates into batched sequential appends [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the system decouples GPU residency from SSD write latency by staging evicted blocks in CPU memory before persisting them, which turns frequent small updates into batched sequential appends. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the section 'Lazy write-back through the CPU cache': 'To avoid frequent small SSD writes, TideGS decouples eviction from VRAM and persistence on SSD. When a dirty block is evicted from VRAM, it is staged to CPU... it is appended to SSD patch segments only when it is later evicted from the CPU cache. This design amortizes write-back and turns frequent block updates into batched sequential appends on the SSD write path...'

Prevents unnecessary persistence of blocks that are still being actively used in VRAM [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'frequently reused dirty blocks may remain resident in CPU memory and are not immediately persisted to SSD' and that the system 'decouples eviction from VRAM and persistence on SSD.' It further explains that when a block is evicted from VRAM, it is staged to the CPU cache, and only flushed to SSD when evicted from the CPU cache or at explicit barriers. This mechanism ensures that blocks actively being used (and thus likely to be accessed again or kept in the CPU cache) are not unnecessarily persisted to the SSD immediately, thereby preventing unnecessary persistence of blocks still in active use.

If the CPU cache is full, evict the least recently used (LRU) block [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the CPU DRAM serves as a cache maintaining an 'LRU cache over blocks' and that the 'LRU policy is updated on each access'. It further clarifies that dirty blocks are flushed (evicted from the CPU cache) 'when they are evicted under CPU memory pressure'. This confirms that when the CPU cache is full (memory pressure), the LRU policy is used to determine which block to evict.

Consistency barriers (checkpointing) may cause latency spikes if many dirty blocks need to be flushed [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'Dirty blocks are flushed to SSD patch segments when they are evicted under CPU memory pressure, or at explicit consistency barriers such as checkpointing and shutdown.' It further explains that this process involves flushing dirty CPU-cache entries. Since flushing many dirty blocks requires I/O operations, and the text highlights that this design is used to amortize writes and avoid random overwrites, the claim that consistency barriers (checkpointing) may cause latency spikes due to the need to flush many dirty blocks is directly supported by the mechanism described (flushing dirty blocks at explicit barriers).
